title: Confusion matrix with exact counts
body:
A confusion matrix lists raw counts for each actual‑vs‑predicted outcome. Look at the four cells to identify true negatives, false positives, false negatives, and true positives.

Here the matrix reports 60 true negatives, 14 false positives, 8 false negatives, and 45 true positives. These exact numbers are the basis for any later metric calculations.

Knowing the counts lets you see whether errors are mainly over‑predictions (false positives) or missed detections (false negatives).

title: How “sat” attends to the sentence
body:
Consider the query token “sat” in the sentence *the cat sat on the mat*. The attention mechanism scores every token relative to this query.

```rh-diagram

```

The largest weight (0.55) goes to the final word “mat”, indicating the model links the action of sitting most strongly with the location.

The next biggest weight (0.20) is on “on”, the preposition that connects the verb to its place.

Smaller contributions come from “cat” (0.10) and the two occurrences of “the” (0.05 each), while the query token itself receives a minimal self‑weight (0.05).

This distribution reflects how the model captures the semantic role of “sat” – primarily its spatial context.
